title: Grid Unchanged After Row Rotations
statement:
You get a grid grid with m rows and n columns, and a number k. Apply this step k times:

  • every row with an even index (0, 2, 4, …) rotates left by one: its first value moves to the end,
  • every row with an odd index rotates right by one: its last value moves to the front.

Return true if, after all k steps, the grid is exactly the same as it was at the start, and false otherwise.

examples.why: k = 2 is not a multiple of the width 4, but every row repeats with period 2, so rotating by 2 brings each row back.
Rotating a row of width 3 by 6 is two full turns, whatever the direction.
The first two rows survive, but the last row becomes [3, 1, 3, 3]. One changed row is enough to answer false.

hints: Does it matter whether a row turns left or right, if all you want to know is whether it comes back to where it started?
Rotating left by k gives back the row exactly when rotating right by k does. So treat every row the same way.
Row i is unchanged when row[j] === row[(j + k) % n] for every column j. No need to actually rotate anything.

explain.intuition:
The directions are a distraction. A row equals its own left rotation by k exactly when it equals its right rotation by k: rotating right undoes rotating left, so if one leaves the row alone, so does the other. That means the question for every row is the same: does shifting it by k places leave it unchanged?

Shifting by k moves the value at column (j + k) mod n into column j. So the row is unchanged if row[j] === row[(j + k) % n] for every j. Reducing k modulo n is what makes this cheap; it is the same wrap-around arithmetic as a carousel component cycling through slides.
steps: For every row and every column j, compare row[j] with row[(j + k) % n].
pitfalls: Answering only k % n === 0. A row with a repeating pattern, like [1, 2, 1, 2], also comes back for smaller shifts.
Simulating k one-step rotations with shift and push and then comparing against the already-rotated rows instead of a saved copy of the original.
Forgetting the modulo, so j + k runs past the end of the row.

solutions.title: Simulate the rotations
solutions.idea: Copy the grid, rotate each row step by step in its direction k times, then compare with the original.

solutions.title: Compare each cell with the one k places ahead
solutions.idea: Direction does not matter, so a row is unchanged iff row[j] equals row[(j + k) mod n] for every j.

followups: Find the smallest k ≥ 1 that leaves the whole grid unchanged.
Rows now rotate by different amounts, row i by k · (i + 1). What changes?
